pass_a_gloss: (and star is not better than star,) but rather 'differs in glory'; but in the case of things of different kind, whenever someone compares these to one another, then 'better' is said with respect to what differs, just as it has been said of wisdom and of stones. If then the apostle had said 'by so much more the Son goes ahead of the angels', or 'by so much greater he is', there would have been a pretext for you, as of the Son being compared to the angels; but now, saying that he is better and differs by as much as a Son stands apart from servants, he shows him to be other than the nature of the angels; and again, saying him to be the one who founded all things, he shows him to be other than all the things that came to be. And he being other and of a different substance besides the nature of the things that came to be, what comparison or likeness of his substance is there to the things that came to be? For on account of this the Son himself also did not say 'My Father is better than I', so that no one should suppose him foreign to that one's nature; but he said 'greater', not by some magnitude nor by time, but on account of the begetting from the Father himself; except that also in saying 'is greater' he showed again the ownness (proper belonging) of the substance. And the apostle also, not wishing primarily to distinguish the substance of the Word in relation to the things that came to be, said (373) 'having become so much better than the angels'; for it is incomparable, or rather it is other; but looking to the enfleshed economy of the Word and the economy then carried out by him, he wished to show this one not to be like those before, so that by as much as he differs by nature from those sent ahead by him, by so much the more the grace that came from this one and through him would become better than the ministry through angels; for it belonged to servants only to demand the fruits, but to the Son and master to grant the debts and to transfer the vineyard. These things then are sufficient to put to shame those fighting against the truth; but if, because it is written 'having become better', they do not wish to hear 'having become', as said about the Son, as equal to 'is', or to take 'having become' because the better ministry came to be and understand as we said, but think that from this word the Word is said to be a thing come-to-be, let them hear again: if the Son is from the angels, let 'having become' be also of him as of those; and let him differ from them in nothing according to nature, but let them either also themselves be sons, or let that one be an angel; and let all in common sit at the right of the Father, or let the Son also stand with all as a ministering spirit, sent himself also for ministries like theirs; but if Paul separates the Son from the things that came to be, saying 'For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son, I today have begotten you? and again: I will be to him for a father and he will be to me for a son' (lacuna) 'And whenever again he brings in the firstborn.' And he says him firstborn not as those twisting (374) the right things say, ranking this with creation, but since he himself is holding first place in all things (lacuna) marveling they said 'Who is this one arriving from Edom' (continues).
pass_b_english: but rather "differs in glory" (1 Corinthians 15:41). With things of different kinds, however, when someone sets them side by side, then "better" is said of what is different, as it is said of wisdom and of stones (Proverbs 8:11). So if the apostle had said, "By so much more the Son goes before the angels," or "by so much is he greater," you would have had a pretext, on the ground that the Son was being compared with the angels. But as it is, by saying that he is better, and differs by as much as a son stands apart from servants, he shows that he is other than the nature of the angels. And again, by saying that he is the one who laid the foundation of all things (Hebrews 1:10), he shows that he is other than all the things that have come into being. And since he is other than the nature of things that have come into being, and of a different substance, what comparison or likeness can his substance have with the things that have come into being? This is why the Son himself did not say, "My Father is better than I," so that no one would take him to be a stranger to the Father's nature. He said "greater" (John 14:28), not by any size or by time, but because of his begetting from the Father himself. And yet in saying "is greater" he showed once more that the substance is his own.

The apostle too, when he said, "having become so much better than the angels" (Hebrews 1:4), did not mean first of all to set the substance of the Word apart from the things that have come into being; for it admits no comparison, or rather it is something other. He was looking to the Word's economy in the flesh, and to the economy he carried out at that time, and wanted to show that he is not like those who came before. So, by as much as he differs in nature from those he had sent before, by so much more the grace that came from him and through him would be better than the ministry carried out through angels. For it was the part of servants only to demand the fruits, but of the Son and Master to forgive the debts and to hand the vineyard over to others.

These things, then, are enough to shame those who fight against the truth. But perhaps, because it is written "having become better," they will not hear "having become," said of the Son, as equal to "is," nor take "having become" to refer to the better ministry that came about and understand it as we have said; perhaps they think that this word says the Word is a thing that came into being. Then let them hear again. If the Son is one of the angels, let "having become" be said of him as of them, and let him differ from them in nothing by nature. Then either they too are sons, or he too is an angel; and either let them all sit together at the right hand of the Father, or let the Son too stand with all of them as a ministering spirit, himself sent on ministries like theirs. But if Paul sets the Son apart from the things that have come into being, saying, "For to which of the angels did he ever say, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you'? And again, 'I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son'" (Hebrews 1:5) […]

"And when he again brings in the firstborn" (Hebrews 1:6). ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον "διαφέρει ἐν δόξῃ·" ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἑτερογενῶν, ὅταν τις ταῦτα παραβάλῃ
πρὸς ἄλληλα, τότε τὸ κρείττων πρὸς τὸ διαλλάττον λέγεται, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ
τῶν λίθων εἴρηται. εἰ μὲν οὖν εἰρηκὼς ἦν ὁ ἀπόστολος Τοσούτῳ μᾶλλον ὁ Υἱὸς τῶν
ἀγγέλων προάγει, ἢ τοσούτῳ μείζων ἐστὶν, ἦν ἂν ὑμῖν πρόφασις ὡς συγκρινομένου τοῦ
Υἱοῦ πρὸς τοὺς ἀγγέλους· νῦν δὲ λέγων κρείττονα αὐτὸν εἶναι καὶ τοσούτῳ διαφέρειν,
ὅσῳ διέστηκεν Υἱὸς δούλων, δείκνυσιν αὐτὸν ἄλλον εἶναι τῆς τῶν ἀγγέλων φύσεως·
λέγων δὲ πάλιν αὐτὸν εἶναι τὸν θεμελιώσαντα τὰ πάντα, δείκνυσιν αὐτὸν ἄλλον εἶναι
πάντων τῶν γενητῶν· ἄλλου δὲ καὶ ἑτεροουσίου αὐτοῦ ὄντος παρὰ τὴν τῶν γενητῶν
φύσιν, ποία τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ σύγκρισις ἢ ὁμοιότης πρὸς τὰ γενητά; διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ
αὐτὸς ὁ Υἱὸς οὐκ εἴρηκεν Ὁ Πατήρ μου κρείττων μου ἐστὶν, ἵνα μὴ ξένον τις τῆς ἐκείνου
φύσεως αὐτὸν ὑπολάβῃ· ἀλλὰ μείζων εἶπεν, οὐ μεγέθει τινὶ, οὐδὲ χρόνῳ, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν
ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Πατρὸς γέννησιν· πλὴν ὅτι καὶ ἐν τῷ εἰπεῖν Μείζων ἐστὶν ἔδειξε πάλιν τῆς
οὐσίας τὴν ἰδιότητα. καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος δὲ, οὐ τὴν τοῦ Λόγου οὐσίαν προηγουμένως
διακρῖναι θέλων πρὸς τὰ γενητὰ ἔλεγε 373 Τοσούτῳ κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων·
ἀσύγκριτον γὰρ, μᾶλλον δὲ ἄλλο ἐστίν· ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὴν ἔνσαρκον οἰκονομίαν τοῦ Λόγου
βλέπων καὶ τὴν τότε γενομένην παρ' αὐτοῦ οἰκονομίαν, ἠθέλησε δεῖξαι οὐχ ὅμοιον
